title: At the bar
goal: Order drinks and snacks, use *vorrei* and *prendo*, and understand the unwritten rules of the Italian bar.
bekal: tell *un caffè*, *un cappuccino*, and *un caffellatte* apart like an Italian

dialogs.title: Dialogo — Al bar, alle otto di mattina
dialogs.intro: An Italian bar is not a place for beer at night — it's a coffee shop that opens at dawn. Budi orders breakfast.

lines.speaker: Barista:
lines.id: Good morning! What can I get you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Buongiorno. Vorrei un cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore.
lines.id: Good morning. I'd like a cappuccino and a croissant, please.
lines.literal: good-morning. I-would-like a cappuccino and a croissant, for favor.

lines.speaker: Barista:
lines.text: Il cornetto vuoto o con la crema?
lines.literal: the croissant empty or with the cream?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Con la crema, grazie. Quanto costa?
lines.id: With custard, thanks. How much is it?
lines.literal: with the cream, thanks. how-much costs?

lines.speaker: Barista:
lines.text: Tre euro e cinquanta. Al banco o al tavolo?
lines.id: Three euros fifty. At the counter or at a table?
lines.literal: three euro and fifty. at-the counter or at-the table?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Al banco. Perché, al tavolo costa di più?
lines.id: At the counter. Why, does it cost more at a table?
lines.literal: at-the counter. why, at-the table costs of more?

lines.speaker: Barista:
lines.text: Sì, al tavolo c'è il servizio. Ecco il cappuccino.
lines.id: Yes, at a table there's a service charge. Here's your cappuccino.
lines.literal: yes, at-the table there-is the service. here-is the cappuccino.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Grazie. Un'altra cosa: avete l'acqua naturale?
lines.id: Thanks. One more thing: do you have still water?
lines.literal: thanks. an-other thing: you(pl)-have the water natural?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Still. Do I pay now or later?

lines.speaker: Barista:
lines.text: Come vuole. Sono quattro e venti in tutto.
lines.id: As you like. That's four twenty altogether.
lines.literal: how you(formal)-want. are four and twenty in all.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Here you are. Have a nice day!

notes: **Vorrei is the most useful word in this unit.** It means "I would like", with a polite tone, like "could I have". The blunt form is *voglio* (I want) — grammatically correct, but it sounds like a child making demands. Use *vorrei*.
**Prendo is also common and more casual.** Literally "I take": *prendo un caffè*. Among friends it's actually the one you'll hear most, like "I'll have".
**In Italy un caffè means an espresso.** A small cup, one sip, drunk standing at the counter in two minutes. If you want a long American-style coffee, order *un caffè americano* or *un caffè lungo*.

**Cappuccino only until about eleven in the morning.** It's not a written rule, but it's a strong habit: milk is considered breakfast food. Ordering a cappuccino after lunch won't be refused, but it will instantly mark you as a tourist.
**Al banco is cheaper than al tavolo.** Counter prices and table prices really are different, and they're officially posted. In tourist towns the difference can be double.
**Ecco** = "here it is", used when handing something over or finding something. *Ecco a Lei* when giving to someone you address formally, *eccoti* to a friend.
**Acqua naturale vs frizzante.** You'll be asked this every single time you order water in Italy. *Naturale* is still, *frizzante* or *gassata* is sparkling.
**Come vuole** = "as you like", literally "how you want". The informal form is *come vuoi*. A gentle, common way of leaving the choice to the other person.

grammars.title: Ordering — three ways, from most casual to most polite
body: All three are correct. Only the tone changes.
after: Adding *per favore* at the end makes any of them softer still, and is never wrong. If you only have time to learn one pattern from this unit, learn *Vorrei… per favore*.

grammars.title: Numbers 0-20
body: Eleven to sixteen have their own forms; from seventeen the pattern flips around.
after: 11-16 put the unit first, a bit like English "four-teen": *dodici* = "two-ten". From 17 the order flips to "ten-seven": *diciassette*.
*Sei* means "six" **and** "you are". Context tells them apart, and in practice it's never confusing: *sei euro* is clearly not "you are euro".

grammars.title: Prices and money
body: Italians say prices with the word *e* (and) in the middle, where English would say the cents straight after the euros.
after: Notice that *euro* **doesn't take a plural**: *due euro*, not *due euri*. It's an official exception, set when the currency was born.
Italian swaps the comma and the period compared with English: *1.500,00* means one thousand five hundred.

sections.title: An order list that will do for your first month

head: Italiano
What you actually get
rows: espresso with a dash of milk
espresso with lots of frothy milk
espresso with lots of milk, no froth
espresso topped up with hot water
croissant, filled with custard or jam
triangle sandwich on soft white bread

blocks.text: Watch the last trap: *una pasta* at a bar means a pastry, not spaghetti. If you mean pasta the dish, name the kind — *gli spaghetti*, *le penne*, *le lasagne*.

blocks.title: Ready-made sentences
items: *Vorrei un caffè, per favore.* — I'd like an espresso, please.
*Quanto costa?* — How much is it? (one item)
*Posso pagare con la carta?* — Can I pay by card?
*Il conto, per favore.* — The check, please.
